newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan opposition take last Taleban town in north.
newsitem.headline: Afghan opposition take last Taleban town in north.

text.p: Pul-i-Khumri, the last major Taleban-held town in northeastern Afghanistan, fell to opposition forces on Wednesday, witnesses said.

They said opposition forces moved into Pul-i-Khumri, 180 km (112 miles) southeast of Mazar-i-Sharif, at about 4 a.m. (2330 GMT Tuesday) after the purist Islamic militia evacuated toward the town of Baghlan, 30 km (19 miles) to the north.

"Last night at about 11 p.m. (1830 GMT), we launched an attack and pushed them back. They attacked back, but could not hold us. We entered the city at about 4:15 a.m. (2345 GMT Tuesday)," said Sayed Jafar Naderi, an opposition commander.
The Taleban had held the town of Pul-i-Khumri for two weeks after a Taleban column moved north across the Hindu Kush range.

Shortly after they crossed the mountains, opposition forces closed the main highway linking Kabul to the north by capturing the town of Jabal-os-Siraj, the southern gateway to the Salang Pass, leaving the Taleban garrison in Pul-i-Khumri surrounded.
Naderi told reporters he believed many of the stranded Taleban fighters had fled north towards Baghlan, but said he expected Baghlan residents to disarm them and hand them over.
"When they got pushed back, they went to Baghlan, but I am sure they will be handed over. The Baghlanis say they have disarmed 4,000 men," said Naderi.

He said opposition forces had captured a large number of Taleban prisoners, including 12 men he said were of Pakistani origin. He had no word on what had happened to Amir Khan Mutaqi, the Taleban information minister, who was leading the force.
Pul-i-Khumri was quiet on Wednesday morning, with few people on the streets. Some shops were open and there was no evidence of continuing fighting.
The capture of Pul-i-Khumri, the last northeastern town to be held by the Taleban, almost brings to a close the militia's disastrous foray into their opponents' northern strongholds.
When an opposition commander, General Abdul Malik, defected to the Taleban just over two weeks ago, the Taleban swept into the north, moving into the northern capital Mazar-i-Sharif.
But soon after the Taleban arrived in Mazar-i-Sharif, Malik turned against them and drove them from the city after fierce street battles that cost them an estimated 300 dead.

The loss of Pul-i-Khumri brings back the front lines between the Taleban and opposition virtually to where they were in January, but the Taleban have lost their aura of invincibility, as well as many battle-hardened troops, in the process.
